newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH CEN BANK HEAD ATTACKS UNREALISTIC WAGE HOPES.
newsitem.headline: CZECH CEN BANK HEAD ATTACKS UNREALISTIC WAGE HOPES.

text.p: Czech National Bank governor Josef Tosovsky, in a thinly veiled attack on Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, said on Monday that politicians had made implementing austerity measures more difficult by raising wage hopes unrealistically.

Although Tosovsky did not mention the prime minister by name, he referred to promises by politicans in the run up to 1996 elections that the standard of living of Czech citizens could be quickly raised to the European Union average.
Klaus provoked a storm before the last election by promising that wages, which in purchasing power terms are around half the EU average, could double by the year 2000.
"Due to higher expectations it is now more difficult to implement tough measures than if politicians had not been so optimistic," Tosovsky told the Financial Times World Gold Conference in Prague.

Due to a sharp economic slowdown, a depreciation of the Czech crown and falling tax revenues, the government has pledged to take drastic measures to cut public expenditure, promising in particular to slam the brakes on wage growth.

Nominal industrial wages were up 14.7 percent in April while industrial output this year has slowed sharply and the government expects almost no economic growth for the first quarter. May inflation was 6.3 percent year-on-year.
The central bank has consistently warned that wage growth poses a threat to its efforts to keep inflation down.
On Monday, Tosovsky repeated that last summer's sharp monetary squeeze which was tightened further in order to protect the crown, had been partly a response to the sharp growth in wages.
The discount rate was raised to 13 percent from 10.5 on May 27.
